old: argue that the pointers were first set at the new moon of 22 or 23 December 178 BC, and they number the cells one lower than everyone else (see the dial note).
new: argue that the pointers were first set for 22 and 23 December 178 BC: on the 22nd there was a new moon, with an annular eclipse of the Sun and the Moon near apogee, and the 23rd they take as the winter solstice. They number the cells one lower than everyone else (see the dial note) and put that eclipse at the end of their first cell, which is everyone else's second. In the usual numbering, then, month 1 begins at the new moon of October 178 BC, which is the first of the four starts below; the other three are the months after it, tried in case their numbering is read another way.
why: The statement is fair but loose: the new moon was on the 22nd and the 23rd is their solstice, and the note does not say which of its four starts is the proposal. Their section 4.1 and Table 2 of the first paper, and Table 3 and the caption of Figure 11 of the second, put the eclipse of 22 December on the last day of their cell 1, which is the usual cell 2; in JPL's tables that eclipse is the new moon that closes month 2 of the start whose month 1 begins on 23 October 178 BC (`s1_date178.out`).

old: what a start taken at random gives (the median of all 3,711 is 5.58).
new: what a start taken at random gives (the median of all 3,711 is 5.58). With all 22 hours they score 6.03, 6.70, 6.12 and 5.86 h, where the median is 5.89, and adding the Exeligmos dial's 8 or 16 hours moves the longitudes and leaves the scores as they are. In the terms of point 4, at the first of the four the Moon's mean anomaly at the first full moon is 138° further on than in 205 BC and the Sun's 176°, where the thirty starts that fit the hours best have 0° to 25° and 5° back to 42° on. The first paper also allows that the maker began one or two Saros cycles, or one or two Metonic cycles of 235 months, after that date; the four starts moved on by each of those score 5.34 to 6.64 h with the 18 hours. (The 22-hour scores are in `after_check.out`; the rest of this is the second reader's, from this folder's code, `check-2-scripts/s2_with_author_code.out`; the four scores above also came out the same from JPL's tables and the catalogue's ΔT by code of their own, `check-2-scripts/s1_date178.out`.)
why: The four starts cover every reading of the numbering, but not the paper's own allowance that the maker "could have chosen as a starting date one or two Metonic/Saros cycles after this specific date". Those sixteen starts do no better. The 22-hour scores are already in `after_check.out`.

old: I have not read the rest, and they may not hold that the hours were meant to match the sky of the starting date.
new: I have not read the rest. The second reader read both papers through and found no such comparison either. The first paper lists the engraved hours of five cells (its Table 2) and says that the eclipse of 22 December 178 BC began "close to the 1st hour" of the day; it sets no engraved hour against a real time. The later paper says in its introduction that the mechanism "predicted upcoming solar and lunar eclipses with date and hour accuracy", and in its abstract that the eclipses on the dial "are calculated by pure mechanical processing" and "are not documented observed events": on its account the maker set the pointers, turned the mechanism on, and engraved a glyph and "the events' predicted hour" wherever the pointers showed an eclipse. For the hours it refers to a third paper of theirs ("Reconstructing the Antikythera Mechanism lost eclipse events applying the Draconic gearing", 2023, pages 22 to 25), which neither of us has read. On that account the hours are the mechanism's own predictions and not times taken from the sky. What is shown here is only that the engraved hours are no nearer the real full and new moons after December 178 BC than after a month taken at random; whether they agree with the authors' account of how the hours were made is not tested.
why: Read through, the papers say more than the hedge allows for: the authors do state where they think the glyphs and their hours came from, and they send the reader to a third paper for the hours. The note should say that, and say that the third paper is unread.
`hours_run.out` prints no anomalies; the 10.5° is in `hours_after.out` (section B, the line for 187 BC).
